title: Kiss the joy as it flies
word: Kiss the joy as it flies
hookLine: who binds to himself a joy destroys it; who kisses it as it flies lives in eternity's sunrise (Eternity)
tomorrow: a poet says I celebrate myself. vanity, or something holy?

lines: HELD SO TIGHT YOU MISSED IT.
cards: Ever held a perfect moment so tightly, filming it, replaying it, planning the next one, that you half missed it?

Blake has four lines on that, written in his private notebook under the title Eternity: "He who binds to himself a joy / Does the winged life destroy; / But he who kisses the joy as it flies / Lives in eternity's sun rise."
So how do you hold a joy without crushing it? You don't grab it. You kiss it as it flies.

teach.b: Notice the two verbs. Binds is what you do to a captive. Kisses is what you do to someone you love, at the door, before you let them go.
Now look at where eternity sits in those lines. Not later, not after death, but in a sunrise you live in now, the moment you stop binding.
That's Blake's teaching: eternity breaks into time when you love a thing without trapping it. Some readers hear an older story underneath.

In Exodus, God feeds Israel in the wilderness with manna, fresh each morning, enough for the day. Some tried to keep it overnight, and it "bred worms, and stank." A gift for today goes bad when it's hoarded.

It's the same day-sized gift Jesus teaches his followers to ask for: "Give us this day our daily bread." And the stories of Blake's own last days, gathered by his biographer Alexander Gilchrist, say he lived his line.
Ill and near the end, he kept drawing, sketched his wife Catherine and told her she had been an angel to him, and died singing.
He didn't bind the joy. He sang it as it flew.

how: Christians pray the Lord's Prayer, asking for daily bread, and in Jewish tradition the two loaves set out on the Sabbath table recall the manna.

games.q: what does “kiss the joy as it flies” mean?
o: a farewell kiss for a friend leaving on a trip
chasing every thrill before it can disappear
loving a joy as it passes, without trapping it

games.q: the week's poems and their lines: tap the pairs.
p: kiss the joy as it flies

s: Blake's Eternity says the way to keep a joy is to hold it tight
he who binds to himself a joy does the winged life destroy.
in Exodus, manna kept overnight bred worms
it came fresh each morning, enough for that day.
in Wordsworth's sonnet, the world means nature
the world is getting and spending; nature is what we've stopped seeing.

games.q: your roommate of a great year is moving across the country. what fits Blake's Eternity?
o: love the year fully and let her go: binding a joy destroys the winged life.
beg her to stay; a real joy is worth holding onto with both hands.
start pulling back now, so it hurts less when she finally leaves.
games.why: Blake's line is about loving without trapping: he who kisses the joy as it flies lives in eternity's sunrise. pulling back early misses the kiss; clutching kills the flight.

practice: For two minutes, listen to one sound you can't keep: a bird, rain, traffic, someone laughing in another room. Let each bit of it arrive and go without trying to hold on.
If something lovely passes through, notice it, thank it, and let it fly.

wordCard.voice: Kiss the joy as it flies: Blake's picture, in his notebook poem Eternity, of loving a joy without trapping it. Bind it, and the winged life dies.

carryVoice: Your line: kiss it as it flies. Eternity's sunrise is found in the letting go. Two weeks of poets, done.
